planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Big Boston is an improved, larger-headed selection of the older Boston Market butterhead type introduced in the late 19th century.

directions: Big Boston is a large-headed American butterhead heirloom from the late 19th century, bred as a bigger-growing improvement on the older Boston Market lettuce. Direct sow seed shallowly in cool, fertile soil in early spring, thinning plants to give heads 10 to 12 inches of room to fully round out. Outer leaves often blush bronze-red at the margins in cool weather, wrapping a pale, buttery, well-blanched heart that holds its quality longer than many smaller butterheads. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pull outer leaves individually for an extended cut-and-come-again harvest.

common_name: Paris White Cos Lettuce (Classic Self-Folding Romaine Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring in loose, fertile soil; Paris White Cos naturally folds its own leaves to self-blanch the heart without the tying older romaine culture once required.

directions: Paris White Cos is a classic upright romaine heirloom grown in French and American kitchen gardens since at least the 19th century, prized for its self-folding habit that naturally blanches the inner leaves without tying. Direct sow in early spring in loose, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to about 8 to 10 inches so the tall, narrow heads can stand upright without crowding each other. The slightly savoyed outer leaves are pale green, wrapping a crisp, sweet, almost-white heart milder than most modern romaines. Succession sow through the cool season and harvest whole heads once the center feels firm.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil in early spring and keep moisture even through heading; Valmaine was selected from older cos lines specifically to resist the rib tipburn that even watering was found to prevent.

directions: Valmaine is a tipburn-resistant cos lettuce selected for more dependable heading than older romaine lines prone to rib scorch under heat or irregular watering. Direct sow in cool soil in early spring, thinning to roughly 8 to 10 inches, and keep moisture consistent through head formation since uneven watering is what triggers the tipburn this variety was bred to resist. It forms upright, medium-green heads with crisp ribs and the mild flavor typical of classic cos types, standing a bit longer in the field before bolting than many older selections. Harvest whole heads at firm maturity or pull outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop.

common_name: Grosse Blonde Paresseuse Lettuce (Big Blonde Lazy, French Heirloom Butterhead)

planting.note: Direct sow in cool, fertile soil in early spring; Grosse Blonde Paresseuse, French for 'big blonde lazy one,' is named for its unhurried, slow-bolting habit rather than any difficulty to grow.

directions: Grosse Blonde Paresseuse, literally 'big blonde lazy one,' is an old French butterhead heirloom named for its unhurried, slow-bolting habit rather than any trouble to grow. Direct sow in cool, fertile soil in early spring, thinning plants to 10 to 12 inches so the large, pale-green, loosely folded heads have room to form their soft, buttery hearts. It tends to stand in good garden condition longer than many butterheads before turning bitter or running to seed, making it a forgiving choice for gardeners who cannot harvest the moment a head matures. Cut whole heads once the center feels full, or harvest outer leaves through the season.

planting.note: Direct sow thinly in early spring in moist, fertile soil; Unrivalled is a Victorian-era English kitchen garden heirloom grown for dependable heading under cool, short-season conditions.

directions: Unrivalled is an English butterhead heirloom from Victorian-era kitchen garden seed catalogs, grown for dependable, well-formed heads under the cooler, shorter-season conditions typical of British gardens. Direct sow thinly in early spring in moist, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to about 8 to 10 inches apart so each plant can round out into a compact, soft-leaved head. The pale green outer leaves wrap a creamy, tender heart with the mild, buttery flavor typical of older European butterhead types. Succession sow every few weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, since like most butterheads it bolts quickly once hot weather arrives.
